content: Simple bone cysts, also referred to as unicameral or solitary bone cysts, are the most common benign bone lesions in growing children. These cysts can weaken the bone structure, leading to repeated pathological fractures, which are fractures occurring in areas of bone compromised by disease. In some cases, these fractures may result in symptomatic malunion, where the bone heals improperly, causing functional or structural issues. The primary goals of treatment for simple bone cysts are to reduce the risk of pathological fractures, promote cyst healing, and alleviate pain. Despite the availability of numerous treatment options, there is no established consensus on the optimal approach for managing these cysts in children. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and harms of various interventions for treating simple bone cysts in the long bones of children and adolescents. The comparisons of interest included invasive interventions (such as injections, curettage, or surgical fixation) versus non-invasive approaches (such as observation, use of a plaster cast, or activity restriction). Additionally, the review aimed to compare different types of invasive interventions (e.g., injections, drilling, decompression, or surgical fixation) and variations within these categories (e.g., comparing different injection substances like autologous bone marrow versus steroids). The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, with the last search performed in April 2016. The inclusion criteria were randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials evaluating treatments for simple bone cysts in children. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, selected studies, assessed the risk of bias, and extracted data. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE system, and results were summarized using risk ratios (RRs), mean differences (MDs), and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). In the 2017 update of this review, no new randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified for inclusion. However, one ongoing trial was noted, which may be included in future updates. The only included study was a multicenter RCT conducted across 24 sites in North America and India. This trial compared bone marrow injections with steroid (methylprednisolone acetate) injections for treating simple bone cysts. Each group was allowed up to three injections. The trial included 90 children with a mean age of 9.5 years, and results were reported for 77 children at a two-year follow-up. The trial had secure allocation concealment but was at high risk of performance bias and baseline imbalances between groups. Due to these limitations, the quality of evidence was downgraded to low for most outcomes and to very low for outcomes with serious imprecision. The trial provided very low-quality evidence suggesting that fewer children in the bone marrow injection group achieved radiographic healing of their bone cysts at two years compared to the steroid injection group (9/39 versus 16/38; RR 0.55 favoring steroid injection, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.09). However, this result was uncertain and could also be consistent with no difference or a small benefit favoring bone marrow injections. Based on an illustrative success rate of 421 children with healed bone cysts per 1000 treated with steroid injections, this would translate to 189 fewer children (95% CI 303 fewer to 38 more) achieving healing per 1000 treated with bone marrow injections. There was low-quality evidence indicating no significant difference between the two interventions in functional outcomes at two years, as measured by the Activity Scale for Kids (a score ranging from 0 to 100, where higher scores indicate better function; MD -0.90; 95% CI -4.26 to 2.46). Similarly, there was no significant difference in pain levels assessed using the Oucher pain score. For adverse events, there was very low-quality evidence suggesting no differences between the two groups in the rates of subsequent pathological fractures (9/39 versus 11/38; RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.37 to 1.70) or superficial infections (two cases in the bone marrow group). Other outcomes, such as recurrence of the bone cyst, unacceptable malunion, return to normal activities, and participant satisfaction, were not reported. The authors concluded that the available evidence is insufficient to determine the relative effectiveness of bone marrow versus steroid injections for treating simple bone cysts in children. Notably, the rate of radiographic healing of bone cysts at two years was below 50% for both interventions. Bone marrow injections are more invasive, but their benefits remain unclear. Overall, there is a lack of robust evidence to guide the choice of treatment for simple bone cysts in children. Further high-quality, adequately powered RCTs are needed to inform clinical practice.
